Snapshots provide incremental, point-in-time backups of persistent disks. Only changed blocks since the last snapshot are stored, making them space-efficient. Snapshots can be stored in a multi-region location and used to create new disks in any region, enabling cross-region disaster recovery.

Persistent disks can be attached to multiple VMs simultaneously in read-only mode, useful for sharing static datasets or reference data across a fleet of VMs. Write access requires exclusive attachment to a single VM.

Hyperdisk is the next generation of GCP block storage, offering dynamically adjustable IOPS and throughput independently of disk size. Unlike standard persistent disks where performance scales with capacity, Hyperdisk lets you provision exactly the performance you need regardless of storage volume.

question.title: Cloud Operations Suite
question.scenario: An operations team needs to monitor application performance, collect logs, trace requests across microservices, and receive alerts when issues occur.
question.question-text: Which GCP offering provides integrated monitoring, logging, and application performance management?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for GCP's integrated observability platform (formerly called Stackdriver) that bundles monitoring, logging, tracing, error reporting, and alerting into a single unified suite.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Operations Suite (formerly Stackdriver) is an integrated set of tools for monitoring, logging, and observability across GCP and hybrid/multi-cloud environments. It includes Cloud Monitoring for metrics, dashboards, and uptime checks; Cloud Logging for log aggregation and analysis; Cloud Trace for distributed request tracing; and Error Reporting for exception tracking. Cloud Console is the web-based management UI for GCP resources, not an observability platform. Cloud Debugger was a tool for inspecting application state in production (now deprecated), not a comprehensive monitoring suite. Cloud Scheduler is a managed cron job service for scheduling tasks. Only Cloud Operations Suite provides the integrated monitoring, logging, tracing, and alerting described in the scenario.

ul.li: Cloud Monitoring supports over 1,500 built-in metrics from GCP services, custom metrics from your applications, and uptime checks that monitor endpoint availability from multiple global locations. Dashboards are fully customizable and can be defined as code using JSON or Terraform.

Cloud Logging provides centralized log management with log-based metrics (extracting numeric metrics from log entries), log routing (sending logs to different destinations based on filters), and log sinks that export to Cloud Storage, BigQuery, or Pub/Sub for long-term analysis and compliance retention.

Cloud Trace collects latency data from distributed applications, showing the full request path across microservices with timing breakdowns at each hop. This is essential for identifying performance bottlenecks in microservices architectures like the one described in the scenario.

Alerting policies combine metric conditions (threshold, absence, or rate-of-change) with notification channels (email, SMS, PagerDuty, Slack, Pub/Sub, or webhooks). Policies support multi-condition logic, allowing alerts that fire only when multiple conditions are simultaneously true to reduce alert noise.

question.title: Cloud NAT
question.scenario: VMs in a private subnet need to access the internet for software updates and API calls, but should not have external IP addresses for security reasons.
question.question-text: Which GCP service provides outbound internet access for VMs without external IP addresses?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the managed network address translation service that lets VMs with only private IP addresses reach the internet for outbound connections without being directly reachable from the internet.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud NAT (Network Address Translation) allows VMs without external IP addresses to initiate outbound connections to the internet while preventing unsolicited inbound connections. It is a fully managed, software-defined service that scales automatically and does not require dedicated gateway VMs or manual NAT configuration. Cloud Interconnect provides dedicated private connections between on-premises networks and GCP, not outbound internet access for VMs. Cloud VPN creates encrypted tunnels to on-premises or other cloud networks, not internet access. Cloud Router manages dynamic BGP routing between your VPC and external networks, and while Cloud NAT uses Cloud Router as its configuration point, Cloud Router alone does not provide NAT functionality. Only Cloud NAT provides the outbound internet access for private VMs described in the scenario.

ul.li: Cloud NAT is configured on a Cloud Router and operates at the VPC subnet level. It translates the private source IP addresses of outbound packets to one or more external NAT IP addresses. Automatic NAT IP allocation dynamically provisions additional IPs as connection count grows, preventing port exhaustion.

Private Google Access is a related but distinct feature: it allows VMs without external IPs to access Google APIs and services (Cloud Storage, BigQuery, etc.) using internal routing. Cloud NAT is for general internet access; Private Google Access is specifically for Google services. Both can be enabled simultaneously on the same subnet.

Cloud NAT logging records connection events (creation, closure, and errors) to Cloud Logging, providing visibility into which VMs are making outbound connections, to which destinations, and any connection failures. This is valuable for security auditing and troubleshooting.

Cloud NAT supports endpoint-independent mapping, meaning the same internal IP:port combination maps to the same external IP:port regardless of destination. This is important for applications that use protocols requiring consistent source addresses, such as STUN/TURN or certain VPN protocols.

question.title: Filestore
question.scenario: A media production company needs a shared file system accessible from multiple VMs simultaneously for collaborative video editing and rendering.
question.question-text: Which GCP service provides fully managed NFS file shares?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for GCP's fully managed file storage service that provides standard NFS (Network File System) shares, allowing multiple VMs to mount and read/write the same file system concurrently.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Filestore is a fully managed file storage service that provides NFS (v3) file shares accessible from multiple VMs and GKE pods simultaneously. It delivers the shared read/write file system semantics needed for collaborative workflows like video editing and rendering. Cloud Storage FUSE is an adapter that lets you mount Cloud Storage buckets as a file system, but it has eventual consistency and performance limitations that make it unsuitable for high-performance collaborative editing. Persistent Disk provides block storage attached to individual VMs; while it supports multi-reader mode, it cannot provide shared read-write access needed for collaboration. Cloud Storage is object storage accessed via HTTP APIs, not a POSIX-compatible file system. Only Filestore provides the true shared NFS file system the scenario requires.

ul.li: Filestore tiers include Basic (HDD and SSD for development and small production workloads), Zonal (high performance SSD with snapshots), Regional (high availability across zones), and Enterprise (multi-zone replication with 99.99% SLA and snapshots). The tier choice depends on performance needs, availability requirements, and budget.

Enterprise tier provides regional high availability by replicating data across two zones in the same region. If one zone fails, Filestore automatically serves data from the surviving zone, making it suitable for production workloads that cannot tolerate zonal outages.

Filestore integrates natively with GKE through the Filestore CSI driver, allowing Kubernetes pods to mount Filestore instances as PersistentVolumes. This enables shared storage across pods in a GKE cluster for workloads like content management, shared model serving, or distributed training.

For media production workflows, Filestore's consistent low-latency random read/write performance is critical because video editing software (like DaVinci Resolve or Adobe Premiere) requires POSIX file system semantics with locking, random access, and millisecond-level latency that object storage cannot provide.

question.title: Security Command Center
question.scenario: A security team needs centralized visibility into security threats, vulnerabilities, and misconfigurations across their GCP organization.
question.question-text: Which GCP service provides centralized security and risk management for GCP resources?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about GCP's centralized security dashboard that aggregates findings from multiple security services, providing a unified view of threats, vulnerabilities, and misconfigurations across your entire organization.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Security Command Center (SCC) is GCP's centralized security and risk management platform. It discovers and inventories all cloud assets, detects active threats, identifies vulnerabilities and misconfigurations, and provides compliance monitoring, aggregating findings from multiple security services into a single dashboard. Cloud KMS manages encryption keys but does not detect threats or monitor security posture. Cloud IAM controls access permissions but does not provide security visibility or threat detection. Cloud Armor protects HTTP(S) load balancers from DDoS and web attacks but does not provide organization-wide security monitoring. Only Security Command Center provides the centralized security visibility and risk management across an entire GCP organization.

ul.li: SCC Standard tier (free) provides asset inventory, Security Health Analytics (basic misconfiguration detection), and Web Security Scanner. Premium tier adds Event Threat Detection, Container Threat Detection, Virtual Machine Threat Detection, full compliance reporting (CIS, PCI-DSS, NIST), and attack path simulation.

Security Health Analytics automatically scans your GCP environment for common misconfigurations like public Cloud Storage buckets, overly permissive firewall rules, unencrypted disks, and service accounts with admin privileges. Findings include severity ratings and remediation guidance.

Event Threat Detection analyzes Cloud Audit Logs and VPC Flow Logs in near-real-time to detect suspicious activities such as cryptocurrency mining, data exfiltration attempts, brute-force SSH attacks, and anomalous IAM grants. Detected threats generate findings with MITRE ATT&CK framework mappings.

Container Threat Detection monitors GKE workloads for runtime threats including reverse shells, unexpected binary execution, and known malicious library loading. This provides defense-in-depth for containerized applications beyond what static image scanning can catch.

question.title: GPUs and TPUs
question.scenario: A machine learning team needs to train deep learning models faster than is possible with CPUs alone.
question.question-text: Which specialized hardware accelerators does GCP offer for machine learning training workloads?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the two types of hardware accelerators GCP offers: industry-standard graphics processors from NVIDIA and Google's own custom-designed machine learning processors built specifically for neural network workloads.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: GCP offers both NVIDIA GPUs and Google-designed Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) for accelerating ML workloads. GPUs are versatile parallel processors that work with all major ML frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX) and also handle non-ML workloads like rendering and simulation. TPUs are custom ASICs designed by Google specifically for neural network training and inference, optimized for matrix operations that dominate deep learning. Standard CPUs can run ML workloads but are orders of magnitude slower for training large models. "ASICs only" is partially correct (TPUs are ASICs) but misses GPUs, which are the more widely used accelerator. GCP does not offer FPGAs as a managed accelerator service. The answer is GPUs and TPUs together.

ul.li: GCP offers multiple NVIDIA GPU types including A100 (80 GB, for large-scale training), H100 (for the most demanding LLM training), L4 (efficient inference and light training), and T4 (cost-effective inference). GPU VMs are available in A2, A3, and G2 machine families, each optimized for different GPU types.

TPU v4 and v5 pods can provide petaflops of computing power, purpose-built for TensorFlow, JAX, and PyTorch workloads. TPU pods consist of thousands of interconnected TPU chips with a high-bandwidth custom interconnect, enabling distributed training of the largest foundation models.

Cloud TPUs are available on-demand, through committed reservations, or via Vertex AI's managed training service. For experimentation, TPU VMs provide direct SSH access, while for production training, Vertex AI handles provisioning, monitoring, and failure recovery automatically.

Choosing between GPUs and TPUs depends on the workload: GPUs offer broader framework compatibility and flexibility (plus non-ML uses), while TPUs provide higher performance-per-dollar for large-scale training workloads that fit TPU-optimized patterns (dense matrix operations, large batch sizes). Many organizations use GPUs for prototyping and TPUs for production training at scale.

question.title: Cloud Console and CLI
question.scenario: A new GCP user needs to manage their cloud resources using both graphical and command-line interfaces.
question.question-text: What are the two primary interfaces for managing GCP resources?

choices.choice: Cloud Console (web UI) and gcloud CLI

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the two primary management interfaces Google provides: a web-based graphical console and an installable command-line tool that together cover interactive and scriptable resource management.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The Cloud Console is a web-based graphical interface for managing GCP resources with dashboards, forms, and visualizations, ideal for exploration and visual management. The gcloud CLI is a command-line tool for scripting, automation, and efficient resource management from any terminal. Both can manage the same resources and are the two primary interfaces Google provides. SSH is a protocol for connecting to Linux VMs, not a GCP management interface. FTP is a file transfer protocol with no GCP management capabilities. REST APIs underlie all interfaces but are not a primary user-facing management tool (they are used by the console, CLI, and client libraries internally). Terraform is a third-party IaC tool, not a Google-provided primary management interface.

ul.li: Cloud Console includes Cloud Shell for terminal access directly in the browser, providing immediate gcloud CLI access without local installation. It also includes the Cloud Shell Editor (web-based IDE) for editing configuration files and code alongside terminal commands.

The gcloud CLI is part of the Google Cloud SDK, which also includes gsutil (Cloud Storage operations), bq (BigQuery operations), and kubectl (Kubernetes operations). Together these specialized tools cover the most common GCP management tasks from the command line.

Client libraries for Python, Java, Go, Node.js, C#, Ruby, and PHP provide programmatic access to GCP services for building applications that interact with cloud resources. These libraries call the same REST/gRPC APIs that the Console and gcloud use under the hood.

Infrastructure as Code tools like Terraform (multi-cloud) and Config Connector (Kubernetes-native) enable declarative resource management through version-controlled configuration files. While not primary interfaces, they are the recommended approach for managing production infrastructure reproducibly.

question.title: Data Transfer Options
question.scenario: A company needs to migrate 100 TB of data from their on-premises data center to Cloud Storage as quickly as possible.
question.question-text: Which GCP service enables offline data transfer for large datasets using physical appliances?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the physical hardware device that Google ships to your location, allowing you to load data locally and ship it back for upload to Cloud Storage, bypassing network bandwidth limitations entirely.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Transfer Appliance is a secure, high-capacity physical storage device that Google ships to your location. You load your data onto it, ship it back to Google, and they upload the data to Cloud Storage. For 100 TB of data, this is often faster than network transfer because it bypasses bandwidth constraints entirely. Storage Transfer Service is for online transfers from other cloud providers (AWS S3, Azure Blob), HTTP/HTTPS sources, or between Cloud Storage buckets, but requires network bandwidth for the transfer. gsutil is a command-line tool for Cloud Storage operations that works for smaller transfers but would take extremely long for 100 TB over typical internet connections. Cloud Interconnect provides a dedicated network link but still requires time proportional to bandwidth. Only Transfer Appliance provides the offline, physical transfer path for massive datasets.

ul.li: Transfer Appliance is available in 100 TB and 480 TB capacities (raw, usable capacity is slightly less). For the 100 TB scenario, a single appliance handles the full dataset. Data is encrypted at rest with AES-256 before it leaves your site, and the encryption key is managed separately from the appliance for security.

The total timeline for a Transfer Appliance engagement is typically 2-4 weeks: order and shipping (days), data loading (depends on local network speed), return shipping (days), and data upload at Google (days). Even with this overhead, it is faster than transferring 100 TB over a 1 Gbps link, which would take approximately 10 days of continuous transfer.

Storage Transfer Service is the right choice for ongoing or one-time online transfers from AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, or HTTP sources. It supports scheduled transfers, bandwidth throttling, and file filtering. For cloud-to-cloud migration, it is usually the simplest option.

Transfer Service for On Premises handles large-scale, ongoing file-based transfers from on-premises systems to Cloud Storage using software agents installed in your data center. It is optimized for petabyte-scale migrations where data continues to change during the migration window and supports incremental transfers.

question.title: Shared VPC
question.scenario: An organization has multiple projects that need to share a common network infrastructure while maintaining separate billing and IAM for each project.
question.question-text: Which GCP feature allows multiple projects to use a common VPC network managed by a host project?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the GCP networking feature that designates one project as the network owner (host) and lets other projects (service projects) deploy resources into the shared network while keeping their own billing and IAM.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Shared VPC allows an organization to connect resources from multiple service projects to a common VPC network owned by a host project. This enables centralized network administration (firewall rules, subnets, routes managed in one place) while each project maintains separate billing, IAM, and resource management. VPN Gateway creates encrypted tunnels to external networks, not shared internal networks across projects. VPC Peering connects two separate VPC networks for private communication, but each project still manages its own network independently without centralized control. Cloud Router handles BGP routing between your VPC and external networks. Only Shared VPC provides the centralized host-project network model with service project resource deployment.

ul.li: The host project owns the Shared VPC network, subnets, firewall rules, routes, and VPN/Interconnect connections. Network administrators in the host project control all networking configuration centrally, ensuring consistent security policies and IP address management across the organization.

Service projects contain the actual workload resources (VMs, GKE clusters, Cloud SQL instances) that use subnets from the shared network. Subnet-level IAM permissions control which service projects can deploy resources into which subnets, enabling network segmentation by environment or team.

A key difference between Shared VPC and VPC Peering: Shared VPC provides a single shared network with centralized management, while VPC Peering connects two independent VPC networks that are each managed separately. Shared VPC is preferred when you want one team to control all networking; VPC Peering is preferred when teams need independent network management.

Shared VPC works within a single organization. The host project and all service projects must belong to the same GCP organization. Cross-organization network sharing requires VPC Peering or Cloud VPN. Shared VPC supports up to 1,000 service projects per host project.

question.title: Organization Policies
question.scenario: A company's security team needs to enforce that no one in the organization can create public Cloud Storage buckets, regardless of their IAM permissions.
question.question-text: Which GCP feature allows administrators to set constraints on how resources can be configured across an organization?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the GCP governance feature that sets organization-wide constraints on resource configurations, operating independently of IAM permissions to enforce rules like "no public storage buckets" regardless of who tries.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Organization Policy Service allows centralized control over how cloud resources can be configured through constraints that apply regardless of IAM permissions. Unlike IAM (which controls who can do what), organization policies control what can be done, period. For example, the constraint constraints/storage.uniformBucketLevelAccess forces uniform access on all buckets, while constraints/iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains restricts which domains can be granted access. Access Context Manager defines access levels (IP ranges, device attributes) used by VPC Service Controls, not resource configuration constraints. Cloud IAM controls identity-based permissions but cannot override itself to prevent all users from a specific action. VPC Service Controls restrict API access context, not resource configuration rules. Only Organization Policy Service enforces configuration constraints organization-wide.

ul.li: List constraints restrict which values are allowed for a resource property (e.g., constraints/gcp.resourceLocations restricts which regions resources can be created in). Boolean constraints enable or disable a capability entirely (e.g., constraints/compute.disableSerialPortAccess blocks all serial port access across the organization).

Organization policies inherit downward through the hierarchy (Organization > Folder > Project) and can be overridden at lower levels unless the parent policy explicitly prevents it. This enables a pattern where the security team sets organization-wide defaults and specific teams can request exceptions at the project level with approval.

Common security constraints include: disabling VM external IP addresses (compute.vmExternalIpAccess), restricting service account key creation (iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation), enforcing uniform bucket-level access (storage.uniformBucketLevelAccess), and restricting public access to Cloud Storage (storage.publicAccessPrevention).

Custom organization policy constraints (using the Custom Constraints feature) let you define your own rules beyond the built-in constraints. For example, you could require that all Compute Engine VMs use a specific minimum machine type, or that all Cloud SQL instances have backups enabled. This extends governance to organization-specific requirements.

question.title: Container Registry and Artifact Registry
question.scenario: A development team needs a secure place to store and manage their Docker container images for deployment to GKE.
question.question-text: Which GCP service provides a managed repository for storing container images and other artifacts?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for GCP's managed artifact repository service that stores Docker container images alongside other package formats, with built-in vulnerability scanning and IAM-based access control.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Artifact Registry is a fully managed, private repository for storing container images and language packages (Maven, npm, Python, Go, and more). It provides IAM-based access control, automatic vulnerability scanning to identify CVEs in container images, and tight integration with CI/CD tools like Cloud Build. Cloud Build is a CI/CD platform that builds and tests code, but it stores artifacts in Artifact Registry, not within itself. Cloud Storage is generic object storage; while Container Registry historically stored images in Cloud Storage buckets behind the scenes, Cloud Storage itself is not a container registry. Source Repositories hosts Git source code, not built container images. Only Artifact Registry provides the dedicated artifact repository with container-specific features the scenario needs.

ul.li: Artifact Registry replaced the legacy Container Registry, adding support for multiple artifact formats beyond Docker images. New projects should always use Artifact Registry. Existing Container Registry users should migrate, as Container Registry is in maintenance mode.

Automatic vulnerability scanning (via Container Analysis) identifies known CVEs in container images when they are pushed to the registry. It continuously monitors for newly discovered vulnerabilities in previously scanned images and can be combined with Binary Authorization to block deployment of images with critical vulnerabilities.

Remote repositories cache packages from public registries (Docker Hub, Maven Central, npm, PyPI) within your Artifact Registry, providing faster builds, reducing external dependency on public registries, and creating an audit trail of which external packages are used in your organization.

Virtual repositories aggregate multiple underlying repositories (standard and remote) behind a single endpoint, simplifying client configuration. Developers configure a single repository URL, and Artifact Registry resolves packages from the correct underlying repository based on configurable priority rules.

question.title: Cloud Build
question.scenario: A development team wants to automate building container images and running tests whenever code is pushed to their repository.
question.question-text: Which GCP service provides a serverless CI/CD platform for building, testing, and deploying applications?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about GCP's serverless CI/CD service that automatically triggers builds from source repository events, executing build steps defined in configuration files on Google-managed infrastructure.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Build is a fully managed CI/CD platform that executes builds on Google's infrastructure. It imports source code from repositories, builds container images, runs tests, and deploys to targets like GKE, Cloud Run, or App Engine. Build configurations define a pipeline of container-based steps that execute sequentially or in parallel. Cloud Composer is a managed Apache Airflow service for orchestrating data pipelines and workflows, not for building and testing application code. Cloud Deploy provides managed continuous delivery specifically for deploying to GKE and Cloud Run but does not handle building or testing. Cloud Scheduler triggers jobs on a cron schedule but does not build, test, or deploy code. Only Cloud Build provides the full CI/CD pipeline from source to deployment.

ul.li: Build triggers automatically start builds when code is pushed to Cloud Source Repositories, GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket. Triggers can filter by branch, tag, or file path changes, and can be configured with substitution variables for dynamic build configuration.

The cloudbuild.yaml (or cloudbuild.json) file defines build steps, each running in a specified container image. Steps share a /workspace directory for passing files between them. Google provides pre-built builder images for common tasks (docker, gcloud, npm, maven, gradle), and you can use any public or private container image as a build step.

Private pools provide dedicated, VPC-connected build workers for builds that need to access private resources (like private registries, internal APIs, or databases) or require consistent build environments. Private pool workers run in your VPC, unlike default workers that run in Google's infrastructure.

Cloud Build integrates with Cloud Deploy for managed continuous delivery, creating a complete CI/CD pipeline. Cloud Build handles the CI (build, test, create artifacts), and Cloud Deploy handles the CD (progressive rollout to dev, staging, production GKE/Cloud Run targets with approval gates and rollback capabilities).

question.title: Object Lifecycle Management
question.scenario: A company stores log files in Cloud Storage and wants to automatically move them to cheaper storage after 30 days and delete them after one year.
question.question-text: Which Cloud Storage feature automates transitioning objects between storage classes or deleting them based on conditions?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the Cloud Storage feature that lets you define rules to automatically change storage classes or delete objects based on conditions like age, matching the automatic tiering and deletion described in the scenario.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Object Lifecycle Management lets you define rules that automatically transition objects to different storage classes or delete them based on configurable conditions. For the scenario, you would create two rules: one to change the storage class to Nearline or Coldline after 30 days, and another to delete objects after 365 days. Object Versioning preserves previous versions of overwritten or deleted objects but does not automate storage class transitions or scheduled deletion. Retention Policies prevent object deletion before a specified age (the opposite of automatic deletion) for compliance purposes. Bucket Lock makes a retention policy permanent and irreversible. Only Object Lifecycle Management provides the automatic transition and deletion based on age.

ul.li: Lifecycle rules support two actions: SetStorageClass (transition to a specified class) and Delete. Conditions include age (days since creation), createdBefore (absolute date), matchesStorageClass, numNewerVersions (for versioned objects), isLive (live vs. noncurrent versions), and daysSinceNoncurrentTime.

Rules apply to all objects in the bucket that match the conditions; you cannot target specific individual objects. If you need different lifecycle policies for different types of objects, store them in separate buckets or use object name prefix conditions available in newer lifecycle rule configurations.

Cloud Storage evaluates lifecycle rules asynchronously, typically once per day. Changes may take up to 24 hours to apply after conditions are met. This means objects may briefly exist past their intended transition or deletion time, which is usually acceptable for cost optimization but important to understand for compliance scenarios.

A common cost optimization pattern chains multiple transitions: Standard (0-30 days) > Nearline (30-90 days) > Coldline (90-365 days) > Delete (365+ days). Each transition respects the minimum storage duration of the target class, so transitioning to Nearline at 30 days aligns with Nearline's 30-day minimum storage requirement.

question.title: Private Google Access
question.scenario: VMs without external IP addresses need to access Google APIs like Cloud Storage and BigQuery without routing traffic through the public internet.
question.question-text: Which feature allows VMs with only internal IPs to reach Google APIs and services?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the subnet-level feature that enables VMs with only internal IP addresses to reach Google APIs and services through internal routing, without needing external IP addresses or Cloud NAT.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Private Google Access allows VMs with only internal IP addresses to reach Google APIs and services (Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Container Registry, etc.) using internal routing rather than the public internet. It is enabled at the subnet level and works transparently with no changes to application code or DNS. Cloud VPN creates encrypted tunnels to on-premises or other cloud networks, not to Google APIs. Cloud NAT provides general outbound internet access for private VMs, but Private Google Access is more efficient and specific for reaching Google services because traffic stays on Google's internal network. VPC Peering connects two VPC networks together, not VMs to Google APIs. Only Private Google Access provides the direct internal path to Google services for private VMs.

ul.li: Private Google Access is enabled per-subnet in the VPC configuration. When enabled, VMs in that subnet can reach Google API endpoints (like storage.googleapis.com) using their internal IP as the source address, with traffic routed through Google's internal network rather than the public internet.

Private Service Connect takes this further by creating private endpoints (internal IP addresses) within your VPC for Google APIs and services. Instead of accessing public API endpoints, your applications connect to a private IP in your VPC, providing even more control over routing and DNS resolution.

Cloud NAT and Private Google Access serve different purposes and can coexist: Private Google Access handles traffic to Google APIs, while Cloud NAT handles traffic to the general internet. A VM with Private Google Access enabled can reach Cloud Storage without Cloud NAT, but needs Cloud NAT to reach external websites like GitHub or package registries.

On-premises hosts can access Google APIs privately through Cloud VPN or Cloud Interconnect combined with Private Google Access. This enables hybrid architectures where on-premises applications securely access GCP services like BigQuery or Cloud Storage without exposing traffic to the public internet.

question.title: IAM Roles Types
question.scenario: A company needs to grant specific permissions to team members, some needing full access to certain services while others need custom combinations of permissions.
question.question-text: What are the three types of IAM roles in GCP?

choices.choice: User, group, and service account roles

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the three categories of IAM roles: broad legacy roles that span all services, Google-managed per-service roles, and roles you define yourself with exactly the permissions you choose.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: GCP IAM has three role types: Basic (primitive) roles are broad permissions (Owner, Editor, Viewer) that apply across all services in a project and are considered legacy because they grant far more permissions than most users need. Predefined roles are Google-managed collections of permissions specific to individual services (like roles/storage.objectViewer or roles/bigquery.dataEditor), providing granular access that follows least-privilege principles. Custom roles let you create your own permission combinations for maximum precision when predefined roles are either too broad or do not match your exact requirements. Options A and D describe identity types and resource levels respectively, not role types. Option C describes access patterns, not the actual IAM role classification system.

ul.li: Basic roles are legacy and should be avoided in production. The Editor role alone includes thousands of permissions across all services, violating least-privilege. Google recommends replacing basic roles with predefined roles using IAM Recommender, which analyzes 90 days of actual permission usage to suggest tighter bindings.

Predefined roles follow the naming convention roles/service.roleName (e.g., roles/storage.objectViewer, roles/compute.instanceAdmin). Google automatically updates predefined roles when new permissions are added to a service, ensuring they stay current without administrator action.

Custom roles can only include permissions that exist in predefined roles. They can be defined at the organization or project level and are useful when you need a unique combination of permissions that no predefined role provides, such as allowing a CI/CD pipeline to deploy containers but not delete them.

IAM policy binding is separate from role types: you bind an identity (user, group, service account, or domain) to a role at a specific resource level (organization, folder, project, or individual resource). The same role can be bound at different levels with different scope, and permissions inherit downward through the resource hierarchy.

question.title: Anthos
question.scenario: An enterprise wants to run their containerized applications consistently across their on-premises data center, GCP, and AWS while using a single management interface.
question.question-text: Which Google platform enables consistent application management across on-premises, GCP, and other clouds?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about Google's multi-cloud and hybrid application platform that extends GCP's managed Kubernetes, service mesh, and configuration management to on-premises, AWS, Azure, and other environments through a single control plane.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Anthos is a managed application platform that extends Google Cloud services and engineering practices to hybrid and multi-cloud environments. It provides a consistent Kubernetes-based development and operations experience across GCP, on-premises data centers, AWS, and Azure through a unified management interface. Cloud Run is a serverless container platform limited to GCP (and Cloud Run for Anthos, which is part of Anthos). GKE is the managed Kubernetes service on GCP only; it does not extend to on-premises or other clouds by itself. "Kubernetes Engine" is just another name for GKE and has the same limitation. Only Anthos provides the multi-cloud and hybrid consistency described in the scenario with a single management plane.

ul.li: Anthos clusters on VMware and bare metal enable running GKE-consistent Kubernetes on-premises, with the same APIs, security model, and management tools as GKE on GCP. Anthos attached clusters bring existing third-party Kubernetes clusters (EKS, AKS, or self-managed) under Anthos management without rebuilding them.

Anthos Service Mesh (based on Istio) provides traffic management, mutual TLS encryption, and observability across all clusters regardless of location. This enables consistent security policies and traffic routing across on-premises, GCP, and other cloud environments.

Anthos Config Management enables GitOps-style cluster configuration, where the desired state of all clusters is defined in a Git repository. Changes committed to the repo are automatically applied to all registered clusters, ensuring configuration consistency and providing an audit trail of every change.

Binary Authorization enforces deploy-time security policies across all Anthos clusters, requiring that container images are signed by trusted authorities before they can run. This provides a consistent security gate for container deployments regardless of where the cluster is running.

question.title: Deployment Manager
question.scenario: A DevOps team wants to define their GCP infrastructure in configuration files that can be version-controlled and repeatedly deployed.
question.question-text: Which GCP service allows you to create and manage cloud resources using declarative YAML or Python templates?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about GCP's native infrastructure-as-code service that lets you define all your cloud resources in declarative YAML or Python template files, creating and managing them as a single deployment unit.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Deployment Manager is an infrastructure deployment service that automates the creation and management of GCP resources using declarative configuration. You define resources in YAML configuration files (or Python/Jinja2 templates for dynamic generation), and Deployment Manager creates, updates, or deletes them as a single atomic deployment. Cloud Build is a CI/CD platform for building and testing code, not for declarative infrastructure management. Cloud Composer is a managed Apache Airflow service for orchestrating data workflows, not infrastructure provisioning. Config Connector is a Kubernetes-native alternative that uses Kubernetes resource definitions to manage GCP resources, not YAML/Python templates in the Deployment Manager format. Only Deployment Manager uses the YAML/Python template approach described.

ul.li: Templates can use Python or Jinja2 for dynamic configuration generation, enabling parameterized, reusable infrastructure definitions. Python templates are more powerful (loops, conditionals, API calls), while Jinja2 templates are simpler for straightforward parameterization.

Deployments can be previewed before applying changes, showing what resources would be created, updated, or deleted without actually making changes. This provides a safety net similar to Terraform's plan command, reducing the risk of unintended infrastructure modifications.

Config Connector is a newer Kubernetes-native alternative that manages GCP resources using Kubernetes Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs). If your team already manages workloads through Kubernetes, Config Connector provides a consistent kubectl-based workflow for both application and infrastructure management.

Many GCP teams now prefer Terraform (with the Google Cloud provider) for infrastructure as code because it supports multi-cloud environments, has a larger community, and provides more sophisticated state management. Deployment Manager remains useful for GCP-only environments and is still supported, but Terraform has become the industry standard for IaC.

question.title: GCP Free Tier
question.scenario: A student wants to learn GCP without incurring costs, using free resources for small-scale projects and experimentation.
question.question-text: What does GCP's Free Tier provide to new users?

choices.choice: Free credits only for certified professionals
$300 credit for 90 days plus always-free tier resources
Free access only during business hours
Unlimited free access to all services for one year

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the two components of GCP's Free Tier: a time-limited credit for trying any service, plus a set of always-free product quotas that never expire and are available to all accounts.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: GCP's Free Tier includes two components: $300 in credits valid for 90 days that new users can spend on any GCP service to explore the platform, plus Always Free tier products that provide limited free usage of certain services indefinitely (no expiration). Option A is wrong because the free trial is available to anyone, not just certified professionals. Option C is wrong because there are no time-of-day restrictions on free tier access. Option D is wrong because access is limited by credit amount and specific service quotas, not unlimited, and the Always Free tier has no one-year expiration. Only option B correctly describes both the $300/90-day trial and the perpetual Always Free resources.

ul.li: Always Free products include: 1 e2-micro VM instance (in select US regions), 5 GB of Cloud Storage (regional, Standard class), 1 GB of Firestore storage with 50K reads/20K writes/20K deletes per day, and 10 GB of BigQuery storage with 1 TB of queries per month. These quotas reset monthly and never expire.

Cloud Functions provides 2 million invocations, 400,000 GB-seconds of compute time, and 200,000 GHz-seconds of CPU time per month for free. Cloud Run provides 2 million requests, 360,000 GB-seconds of memory, and 180,000 vCPU-seconds per month for free. These serverless free tiers are generous enough for learning and small production workloads.

During the 90-day free trial, GCP will not charge your credit card even if you exceed the $300 credit; resources are simply shut down. After the trial, you must explicitly upgrade to a paid account to continue using resources beyond the Always Free quotas, preventing surprise charges for students and learners.

Budget alerts should be set up even on free tier accounts to monitor spending against the $300 credit and to provide early warning if Always Free quotas are being approached after the trial ends. The combination of free tier resources and billing alerts makes GCP accessible for learning without financial risk.

term.name: GCP (Google Cloud Platform)
term.definition: A suite of cloud computing services running on the same infrastructure that Google uses internally for its end-user products.
term.exam-note: GCP is often used interchangeably with Google Cloud.

term.name: Compute Engine
term.definition: GCP's Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) offering that provides virtual machines running on Google's infrastructure.
term.exam-note: Know the difference between Compute Engine (IaaS), App Engine (PaaS), and Cloud Functions (FaaS).

term.name: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)
term.definition: A managed Kubernetes service for deploying, managing, and scaling containerized applications.
term.exam-note: GKE Autopilot mode provides fully managed node operations.

term.name: Cloud Storage
term.definition: Object storage service for storing and accessing data on Google's infrastructure with high durability and availability.
term.exam-note: Remember the four storage classes: Standard, Nearline, Coldline, and Archive.

term.name: BigQuery
term.definition: A serverless, highly scalable enterprise data warehouse designed for business agility with built-in machine learning.
term.exam-note: BigQuery separates storage and compute, enabling independent scaling.

term.name: Virtual Private Cloud (VPC)
term.definition: A global, software-defined network that provides networking for GCP resources with firewall rules, routing, and private connectivity.
term.exam-note: VPCs are global; subnets are regional.

term.name: Identity and Access Management (IAM)
term.definition: The system for managing access to GCP resources by defining who (identity) has what access (role) to which resources.
term.exam-note: Understand the difference between basic, predefined, and custom roles.

term.name: Cloud Run
term.definition: A fully managed compute platform that runs stateless containers and automatically scales them based on incoming requests.
term.exam-note: Cloud Run can scale to zero and charges only for request processing time.

term.name: Cloud Pub/Sub
term.definition: A fully managed messaging service for building event-driven systems with at-least-once delivery guarantees.
term.exam-note: Pub/Sub decouples senders and receivers, enabling asynchronous communication.

term.name: Cloud SQL
term.definition: A fully managed relational database service for MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server.
term.exam-note: Cloud SQL handles backups, replication, and patching automatically.
